\begin{abstract}
Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation over document collections can answer a question from optical character recognition (OCR) text, from a
retrieved page image, or from both, at very different GPU cost. At scale this is a resource-scheduling problem.
Generation dominates per-query compute, so sending every query through the most expensive path inflates the number
of accelerators needed to meet a latency target; and late-interaction visual indexes grow with the corpus, to
24.6\,GiB at 100k pages and about 246\,GiB at a million. We present the Cost-Aware Visual Router (CAVR), which
chooses the answer path per query with a cost weight set at serving time. On one RTX 4090, we run every path on
8,150 DocVQA and InfographicVQA questions with real BM25 and ColPali retrieval and a local vision-language
generator, and measure answer quality as average normalised Levenshtein similarity (ANLS), GPU-seconds, energy and latency per query. Routers are evaluated on
held-out pages of five splits (about 1,600 questions each). A content-aware router, CAVR-CE, whose cross-encoder (CE) reads the
retrieved passages before generation, uses 29\% less GPU compute than always using both contexts. Its ANLS
is lower by 0.008 on average (paired; lower on 4 of 5 splits, significant on
2), and the exact-match difference is not significant on 5 of 5. In a load test
simulated from measured service times, it cuts the GPUs needed for 100 queries/s at a p95 latency of 2\,s from
106 to 72. We also show that the keyword-derived labels of our earlier
version are uncorrelated with which path actually answers correctly, that a per-query oracle leaves large headroom,
and how visual-index latency scales to 100k pages. Measured on two further nodes, with three Tesla P40 and two NVIDIA A10 GPUs, sharding the
visual index scales near-linearly: a 150k-page index (36.9\,GiB) is searched in the time one GPU
needs for 50k pages. Held in host memory instead, an index of a million pages (246\,GiB) is
searched by two GPUs in large batches at close to the GPU cost per query of GPU-resident search, which would need
16 GPUs; single queries then take seconds, so this placement suits batch search.
\end{abstract}
